claim: Strain a161 (WT) contains the full complement of seven cox1 and five cob introns.
source: The control strain a161 (WT) contains the full complement of seven cox1 and five cob introns, whereas strain a161-U7 (I0) carries an intronless mitochondrial genome, which was originally constructed by Seraphin and co-workers via serial recombination of natural yeast isolates that lack individual mitochondrial introns (Séraphin et al., 1987).
evidence: Directly stated in the text describing the strains used in the study.

claim: Strain a161-U7 (I0) carries an intronless mitochondrial genome.
source: The control strain a161 (WT) contains the full complement of seven cox1 and five cob introns, whereas strain a161-U7 (I0) carries an intronless mitochondrial genome, which was originally constructed by Seraphin and co-workers via serial recombination of natural yeast isolates that lack individual mitochondrial introns (Séraphin et al., 1987).
evidence: Directly stated in the text with citation to the original construction method.

claim: The intronless mitochondrial genome was originally constructed by Seraphin and co-workers via serial recombination of natural yeast isolates that lack individual mitochondrial introns.
source: The control strain a161 (WT) contains the full complement of seven cox1 and five cob introns, whereas strain a161-U7 (I0) carries an intronless mitochondrial genome, which was originally constructed by Seraphin and co-workers via serial recombination of natural yeast isolates that lack individual mitochondrial introns (Séraphin et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation to Séraphin et al., 1987.

claim: Exponential growth on glucose-supplemented YPD medium is ~30% slower for I0 compared to WT.
source: When the two strains are cultured in isolation, exponential growth on glucose-supplemented YPD medium is ~30% slower for I0 compared to WT (Figure 1a).
evidence: Quantitative measurement reported in text and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: I0 fares poorly when pitted directly against WT in competitive fitness assay.
source: I0 also fares poorly when pitted directly against WT in competitive fitness assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chronological life span (CLS) is almost two-fold longer for I0 compared to WT.
source: Chronological life span (CLS, see Materials and methods), on the other hand, is almost two-fold longer for I0 (Figure 1b).
evidence: Quantitative measurement reported in text and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: I0 displays increased mitochondrial mass and volume.
source: At the cellular level, I0 displays increased mitochondrial mass and volume and a mitochondrial morphology characterized by a large network of branched tubules of homogeneous diameter (Figure 1c–e).
evidence: Experimental observation reported in text and shown in Figures 1c-e.

claim: I0 displays a mitochondrial morphology characterized by a large network of branched tubules of homogeneous diameter.
source: At the cellular level, I0 displays increased mitochondrial mass and volume and a mitochondrial morphology characterized by a large network of branched tubules of homogeneous diameter (Figure 1c–e).
evidence: Morphological observation reported in text and shown in Figures 1c-e.

claim: Transcript levels of mitofusin (fzo1) are strongly upregulated in I0 (4.02-fold, p=0.002).
source: Transcript levels of mitofusin (fzo1) and the GTPase mgm1, key nuclearly encoded regulators of mitochondrial fusion, are strongly upregulated (qPCR, t-test, fzo1: 4.02-fold, p=0.002; mgm1: 5.24-fold, p=3.19×10−5, Figure 2a)
evidence: qPCR measurement with statistical significance reported.

claim: Transcript levels of the GTPase mgm1 are strongly upregulated in I0 (5.24-fold, p=3.19×10−5).

evidence: qPCR measurement with statistical significance reported.

claim: Mitofusin (fzo1) and the GTPase mgm1 are key nuclearly encoded regulators of mitochondrial fusion.
source: Transcript levels of mitofusin (fzo1) and the GTPase mgm1, key nuclearly encoded regulators of mitochondrial fusion, are strongly upregulated (qPCR, t-test, fzo1: 4.02-fold, p=0.002; mgm1: 5.24-fold, p=3.19×10−5, Figure 2a)
evidence: Established knowledge about the function of these genes.

claim: Levels of dnm1 are moderately induced in I0 (1.67-fold, p=0.026).

claim: Levels of fis1 are moderately induced in I0 (1.81-fold, p=0.085).

claim: dnm1 and fis1 orchestrate mitochondrial fission.

claim: The changes in mitochondrial morphology in I0 result from increased fusion rather than impaired fission.
source: suggesting that the changes in mitochondrial morphology result from increased fusion rather than impaired fission.
evidence: Inference based on the differential upregulation of fusion vs. fission genes.

claim: The I0 strain exhibits a 2.7-fold increase in mitochondrial DNA copy number (qPCR, t-test p=1.09×10−7).
source: The I0 strain also exhibits a 2.7-fold increase in mitochondrial DNA copy number (qPCR, t-test p=1.09×10−7).
evidence: qPCR measurement with statistical significance reported.

claim: There are no significant differences in mitochondrial inner membrane potential between I0 and WT, as measured by DiOC6(3) fluorescence.
source: At the same time, there are no significant differences in mitochondrial inner membrane potential, as measured by 3,3'-Dihexyloxacarbocyanine iodide [DiOC6(3)] fluorescence (Figure 1f)

claim: Mitochondria in I0 are functional despite grossly altered morphology.
source: suggesting that mitochondria are functional despite grossly altered morphology.
evidence: Inference based on maintained membrane potential.

claim: I0 retains the capacity to grow on glycerol, a non-fermentable carbon source.
source: This notion is further supported by the observation that I0 retains the capacity to grow on glycerol, a non-fermentable carbon source (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), as previously reported for a different nuclear background (Minczuk et al., 2002).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and supported by citation.

claim: I0 has higher oxygen consumption during exponential growth.
source: In fact, biomarkers of mitochondrial metabolism point to increased mitochondrial activity, with higher oxygen consumption (Figure 1g) and cellular ATP levels (Figure 1h) during exponential growth.
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 1g.

claim: I0 has higher cellular ATP levels during exponential growth.
source: In fact, biomarkers of mitochondrial metabolism point to increased mitochondrial activity, with higher oxygen consumption (Figure 1g) and cellular ATP levels (Figure 1h) during exponential growth.
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 1h.

claim: Levels of mitochondrial superoxide are reduced in I0.
source: Despite increased activity, levels of mitochondrial superoxide are reduced (Figure 1i)
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in Figure 1i.

claim: The mitochondrial ROS-scavenger sod2 is upregulated > 7.5-fold in I0 (qPCR, t-test p=0.003).
source: likely reflecting a > 7.5-fold upregulation of the mitochondrial ROS-scavenger sod2 (qPCR, t-test p=0.003, Figure 2a).
evidence: qPCR measurement with statistical significance reported.

claim: Reduced mitochondrial superoxide levels in I0 likely reflect upregulation of the mitochondrial ROS-scavenger sod2.
source: likely reflecting a > 7.5-fold upregulation of the mitochondrial ROS-scavenger sod2 (qPCR, t-test p=0.003, Figure 2a).
evidence: Inference connecting reduced superoxide to increased sod2 expression.

claim: Intron removal challenges but does not terminally compromise mitochondrial function.
source: Thus, intron removal challenges but does not terminally compromise mitochondrial function.
evidence: Summary inference based on the collection of mitochondrial function measurements.

claim: The phenotypic changes in I0 suggest an involvement of the retrograde response.
source: The phenotypic changes we observe suggest an involvement of the retrograde response, as do upregulation of cit2, upregulation of the two rate-limiting members of the TCA cycle, cit1 and idh1, and upregulation of both mitochondrially (cox1, cox2, atp6) and nuclearly (cox4, atp1, sdh1, sdh2) encoded parts of the respiratory chain (Figure 2a).
evidence: Inference based on gene expression patterns characteristic of retrograde response.

claim: cit2 is upregulated in I0.
source: The phenotypic changes we observe suggest an involvement of the retrograde response, as do upregulation of cit2, upregulation of the two rate-limiting members of the TCA cycle, cit1 and idh1, and upregulation of both mitochondrially (cox1, cox2, atp6) and nuclearly (cox4, atp1, sdh1, sdh2) encoded parts of the respiratory chain (Figure 2a).

claim: cit1 and idh1 are the two rate-limiting members of the TCA cycle.
source: The phenotypic changes we observe suggest an involvement of the retrograde response, as do upregulation of cit2, upregulation of the two rate-limiting members of the TCA cycle, cit1 and idh1, and upregulation of both mitochondrially (cox1, cox2, atp6) and nuclearly (cox4, atp1, sdh1, sdh2) encoded parts of the respiratory chain (Figure 2a).

claim: cit1 and idh1 are upregulated in I0.
source: The phenotypic changes we observe suggest an involvement of the retrograde response, as do upregulation of cit2, upregulation of the two rate-limiting members of the TCA cycle, cit1 and idh1, and upregulation of both mitochondrially (cox1, cox2, atp6) and nuclearly (cox4, atp1, sdh1, sdh2) encoded parts of the respiratory chain (Figure 2a).
evidence: Gene expression data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Mitochondrially encoded parts of the respiratory chain (cox1, cox2, atp6) are upregulated in I0.
source: The phenotypic changes we observe suggest an involvement of the retrograde response, as do upregulation of cit2, upregulation of the two rate-limiting members of the TCA cycle, cit1 and idh1, and upregulation of both mitochondrially (cox1, cox2, atp6) and nuclearly (cox4, atp1, sdh1, sdh2) encoded parts of the respiratory chain (Figure 2a).
evidence: Gene expression data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Nuclearly encoded parts of the respiratory chain (cox4, atp1, sdh1, sdh2) are upregulated in I0.
source: The phenotypic changes we observe suggest an involvement of the retrograde response, as do upregulation of cit2, upregulation of the two rate-limiting members of the TCA cycle, cit1 and idh1, and upregulation of both mitochondrially (cox1, cox2, atp6) and nuclearly (cox4, atp1, sdh1, sdh2) encoded parts of the respiratory chain (Figure 2a).
evidence: Gene expression data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Deletion of rtg2 suppresses the I0 phenotype.
source: Indeed, deletion of rtg2, the transcriptional master regulator of the retrograde response and a sensor of mitochondrial dysfunction, suppresses the I0 phenotype (Figure 3).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 3.

claim: rtg2 is the transcriptional master regulator of the retrograde response and a sensor of mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Indeed, deletion of rtg2, the transcriptional master regulator of the retrograde response and a sensor of mitochondrial dysfunction, suppresses the I0 phenotype (Figure 3).
evidence: Established knowledge about rtg2 function.

claim: Upon deletion of rtg2 in I0, tubular structure is lost and large spherical shapes become prominent.
source: Tubular structure is lost and large spherical shapes become prominent (Figure 3a), suggesting distinct defects in the maintenance of mitochondrial ultrastructure (Paumard et al., 2002; Velours et al., 2009).
evidence: Morphological observation shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Loss of tubular structure and prominence of large spherical shapes suggest distinct defects in the maintenance of mitochondrial ultrastructure.
source: Tubular structure is lost and large spherical shapes become prominent (Figure 3a), suggesting distinct defects in the maintenance of mitochondrial ultrastructure (Paumard et al., 2002; Velours et al., 2009).
evidence: Inference supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Deletion of rtg2 in WT strains has no significant effect on mitochondrial volume and morphology, oxygen consumption and ATP levels.
source: Deletion of rtg2 in WT strains, where the retrograde response is not activated, has no significant effect on mitochondrial volume and morphology, oxygen consumption and ATP levels (Figure 3a–d).
evidence: Experimental observations shown in Figures 3a-d.

claim: The extension of CLS in I0 is abrogated in the absence of rtg2, becoming shorter even than the wildtype.
source: The extension of CLS is abrogated in the absence of rtg2, becoming shorter even than the wildtype (Figure 3e).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 3e.

claim: An intact retrograde response, including upregulation of nuclear components of the respiratory chain, is necessary to generate the mitochondrial phenotype observed in the I0 strain.
source: We conclude that an intact retrograde response, including upregulation of nuclear components of the respiratory chain, is necessary to generate the mitochondrial phenotype observed in the I0 strain.
evidence: Conclusion based on the effects of deleting rtg2 and hap4.

claim: Upon deletion of hap4 in I0, mitochondrial morphology reverts back to the wild-type state.
source: Upon deletion of hap4, the transcriptional activator of nuclearly encoded components of the respiratory chain (as well as the TCA cycle enzymes under normal conditions), mitochondrial morphology reverts back to the wild-type state (Figure 4a–e).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figures 4a-e.

claim: hap4 is the transcriptional activator of nuclearly encoded components of the respiratory chain.
source: Upon deletion of hap4, the transcriptional activator of nuclearly encoded components of the respiratory chain (as well as the TCA cycle enzymes under normal conditions), mitochondrial morphology reverts back to the wild-type state (Figure 4a–e).
evidence: Established knowledge about hap4 function.

claim: hap4 is the transcriptional activator of TCA cycle enzymes under normal conditions.
source: Upon deletion of hap4, the transcriptional activator of nuclearly encoded components of the respiratory chain (as well as the TCA cycle enzymes under normal conditions), mitochondrial morphology reverts back to the wild-type state (Figure 4a–e).
evidence: Established knowledge about hap4 function.

claim: cox1 mRNA levels are strongly elevated in I0 (10.9-fold).
source: For both these genes, mRNA levels are strongly elevated in I0 (10.9-fold and 5.8-fold for cox1 and cob, respectively; Figure 2a)
evidence: qPCR measurement shown in Figure 2a.

claim: cob mRNA levels are strongly elevated in I0 (5.8-fold).
source: For both these genes, mRNA levels are strongly elevated in I0 (10.9-fold and 5.8-fold for cox1 and cob, respectively; Figure 2a)
evidence: qPCR measurement shown in Figure 2a.

claim: cox1 and cob mRNA levels are elevated in ∆rtg2.
source: but also in ∆rtg2 (Figure 3f) and ∆hap4 (Figure 4f), suggesting that this is a direct effect of intron removal rather than a downstream consequence of activating the retrograde response.
evidence: qPCR measurement shown in Figure 3f.

claim: cox1 and cob mRNA levels are elevated in ∆hap4.
source: but also in ∆rtg2 (Figure 3f) and ∆hap4 (Figure 4f), suggesting that this is a direct effect of intron removal rather than a downstream consequence of activating the retrograde response.

claim: Elevated cox1 and cob mRNA levels are a direct effect of intron removal rather than a downstream consequence of activating the retrograde response.
source: but also in ∆rtg2 (Figure 3f) and ∆hap4 (Figure 4f), suggesting that this is a direct effect of intron removal rather than a downstream consequence of activating the retrograde response.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that elevated mRNA levels persist even when retrograde response is disrupted.

claim: Simultaneous attenuation of both cox1 and cob promoters in I0 fully reverses the I0-characteristic suit of morphological and molecular phenotypes.
source: We find that simultaneous attenuation of both promoters in I0 fully reverses the I0-characteristic suit of morphological and molecular phenotypes (see I0pp throughout Figure 5).
evidence: Experimental observation shown throughout Figure 5.

claim: Attenuation of either cob or cox1 in isolation only partially reverses the I0 phenotype.
source: Attenuation of either cob (I0cobp) or cox1 (I0cox1p) in isolation only partially reverses the phenotype, although I0cobp has a larger relative effect than I0cox1p (Figure 5).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 5.

claim: I0cobp has a larger relative effect than I0cox1p in reversing the I0 phenotype.
source: Attenuation of either cob (I0cobp) or cox1 (I0cox1p) in isolation only partially reverses the phenotype, although I0cobp has a larger relative effect than I0cox1p (Figure 5).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 5.

claim: Mss116 is a nuclearly encoded DEAD box RNA helicase.
source: To this end, we overexpressed the nuclearly encoded DEAD box RNA helicase Mss116, which promotes splicing of all S. cerevisiae mitochondrial introns by remodeling or stabilizing splice-relevant RNA structures in an ATP-dependent manner (Karunatilaka et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2005).
evidence: Established knowledge about Mss116 supported by citations.

claim: Mss116 promotes splicing of all S. cerevisiae mitochondrial introns by remodeling or stabilizing splice-relevant RNA structures in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: To this end, we overexpressed the nuclearly encoded DEAD box RNA helicase Mss116, which promotes splicing of all S. cerevisiae mitochondrial introns by remodeling or stabilizing splice-relevant RNA structures in an ATP-dependent manner (Karunatilaka et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2005).
evidence: Established knowledge about Mss116 function supported by citations.

claim: The Mss116 overexpression strain (Mss116OE) phenocopies I0.
source: Remarkably, the Mss116 overexpression strain (Mss116OE) phenocopies I0.
evidence: Summary statement of experimental observations detailed in subsequent text and figures.

claim: Mss116OE exhibits increased generation times.
source: Mss116OE exhibits increased generation times, extended chronological life span, lower competitive fitness, increased mitochondrial fusion, 2.9-fold increased mtDNA copy number (qPCR, t-test p=5.5×10−7), elevated oxygen consumption, and altered ATP and ROS production (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mss116OE exhibits extended chronological life span.
source: Mss116OE exhibits increased generation times, extended chronological life span, lower competitive fitness, increased mitochondrial fusion, 2.9-fold increased mtDNA copy number (qPCR, t-test p=5.5×10−7), elevated oxygen consumption, and altered ATP and ROS production (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mss116OE exhibits lower competitive fitness.
source: Mss116OE exhibits increased generation times, extended chronological life span, lower competitive fitness, increased mitochondrial fusion, 2.9-fold increased mtDNA copy number (qPCR, t-test p=5.5×10−7), elevated oxygen consumption, and altered ATP and ROS production (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mss116OE exhibits elevated oxygen consumption.

claim: Mss116OE exhibits longer replicative life span (RLS).
source: In addition, we observe longer replicative life span (RLS) in Mss116OE (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), a more direct proxy of ageing that we were not able to measure accurately in I0, where separating mother and daughter cells in a timely fashion proved challenging (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Overexpression of a DEAD box mutant of Mss116 (Mss116E268K), which lacks ATPase and therefore helicase activity, does not phenocopy I0.
source: Overexpression of a DEAD box mutant of Mss116 (Mss116E268K), which lacks ATPase and therefore helicase activity, does not phenocopy I0 (Figure 1).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 1.

claim: The role of Mss116 in splicing, which relies on helicase activity, is critical for the phenotype.
source: This suggests that the role of Mss116 in splicing – which relies on helicase activity – is critical rather than a recently suggested ATP-independent role in transcription elongation (Markov et al., 2014).
evidence: Inference based on the observation that the helicase-deficient mutant does not phenocopy I0, with citation to alternative hypothesis.

claim: The fact that Mss116OE phenocopies I0 indicates that the stress phenotype in these strains is not caused by missing DNA-level functionality.
source: More generally, the fact that Mss116OE – which encodes a full complement of introns – phenocopies I0 indicates that the stress phenotype in these strains is not caused by missing DNA-level functionality and instead points toward a critical role for splicing.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that Mss116OE has introns but still shows the phenotype.

claim: The fact that Mss116OE phenocopies I0 points toward a critical role for splicing in the stress phenotype.
source: More generally, the fact that Mss116OE – which encodes a full complement of introns – phenocopies I0 indicates that the stress phenotype in these strains is not caused by missing DNA-level functionality and instead points toward a critical role for splicing.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that both intron deletion and enhanced splicing produce similar phenotypes.

claim: Overexpressing Mss116 in I0 did not reveal additional phenotypes and the strain behaved like I0.
source: Overexpressing Mss116 in I0 did not reveal additional phenotypes and the strain behaved like I0 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) further supporting the notion that intron deletion and Mss116 overexpression act through the same pathway.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Intron deletion and Mss116 overexpression act through the same pathway.
source: Overexpressing Mss116 in I0 did not reveal additional phenotypes and the strain behaved like I0 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) further supporting the notion that intron deletion and Mss116 overexpression act through the same pathway.
evidence: Inference based on the lack of additive effects when combining I0 and Mss116OE.

claim: Deletion of Mss116 in the I0 strain results in the same suite of phenotypes as I0.
source: To test this hypothesis, we deleted Mss116 in the I0 strain. We observe the same suite of phenotypes we see in I0 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), demonstrating that neither absolute nor relative excess of Mss116 are responsible for the stress phenotype described above.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neither absolute nor relative excess of Mss116 are responsible for the stress phenotype in I0 and Mss116OE.
source: We observe the same suite of phenotypes we see in I0 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), demonstrating that neither absolute nor relative excess of Mss116 are responsible for the stress phenotype described above.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that deleting Mss116 in I0 does not change the phenotype.

claim: Most mitochondrial introns are strongly depleted in Mss116OE compared to the empty vector control and relative to exons.
source: We find that most mitochondrial introns are strongly depleted in Mss116OE compared to the empty vector control and relative to exons.
evidence: qPCR and RNA-FISH measurements reported in the text and figures.

claim: The relative depletion of individual introns in Mss116OE is somewhat variable.
source: The relative depletion of individual introns is somewhat variable and one intron – aI5α - is equally abundant in Mss116OE and the Y258 WT (Figure 2a).
evidence: qPCR measurement shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Intron aI5α is equally abundant in Mss116OE and the Y258 WT.
source: The relative depletion of individual introns is somewhat variable and one intron – aI5α - is equally abundant in Mss116OE and the Y258 WT (Figure 2a).
evidence: qPCR measurement shown in Figure 2a.

claim: For both cox1 and cob, Mss116 overexpression shifts the balance between unspliced (or partially spliced) pre-mRNA transcripts towards mature mRNA transcripts.
source: For both cox1 and cob, Mss116 overexpression shifts the balance between unspliced (or partially spliced) pre-mRNA transcripts, which dominate the uninduced steady state, towards mature mRNA transcripts (Figure 2c)
evidence: qPCR time series shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Unspliced (or partially spliced) pre-mRNA transcripts dominate the uninduced steady state for cox1 and cob.
source: For both cox1 and cob, Mss116 overexpression shifts the balance between unspliced (or partially spliced) pre-mRNA transcripts, which dominate the uninduced steady state, towards mature mRNA transcripts (Figure 2c)
evidence: qPCR time series shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Total transcript abundance (mRNA plus pre-mRNA) for cox1 and cob remains largely unchanged upon Mss116 overexpression.
source: while total transcript abundance (mRNA plus pre-mRNA) remains largely unchanged.
evidence: qPCR measurements reported in the text.

claim: Nascent transcriptional output is unchanged in Mss116OE compared to the empty vector control.
source: These observations are consistent with a model where nascent transcriptional output is unchanged in Mss116OE compared to the empty vector control and differential steady state levels are the result of post-transcriptional events.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that total transcript levels remain constant while the ratio of pre-mRNA to mature mRNA changes.

claim: Differential steady state levels of cox1 and cob transcripts in Mss116OE are the result of post-transcriptional events.
source: These observations are consistent with a model where nascent transcriptional output is unchanged in Mss116OE compared to the empty vector control and differential steady state levels are the result of post-transcriptional events.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that total transcript levels remain constant while the ratio of pre-mRNA to mature mRNA changes.

claim: Mss116OE phenocopies I0 because eliminating introns at the DNA level (I0) and facilitating accurate and efficient excision at the RNA level (Mss116OE) both result in abnormally efficient transcript maturation.
source: Based on these findings, we suggest that Mss116OE phenocopies I0 because eliminating introns at the DNA level (I0) and facilitating accurate and efficient excision at the RNA level (Mss116OE) both result in abnormally efficient transcript maturation.
evidence: Inference based on the collection of experimental observations.

claim: Abnormally efficient transcript maturation results in fewer transcripts being eliminated by mitochondrial quality control.
source: That is, fewer transcripts are eliminated by mitochondrial quality control because splicing is erroneous or does not proceed in a timely manner, resulting in a greater number of mature cox1/cob mRNAs.
evidence: Inference explaining the mechanism of abnormally efficient transcript maturation.

claim: Abnormally efficient transcript maturation results in a greater number of mature cox1/cob mRNAs.
source: That is, fewer transcripts are eliminated by mitochondrial quality control because splicing is erroneous or does not proceed in a timely manner, resulting in a greater number of mature cox1/cob mRNAs.
evidence: Inference explaining the consequence of abnormally efficient transcript maturation.

claim: Increased cox1/cob transcript levels are perceived as stressful and trigger the retrograde response.
source: For reasons that remain to be elucidated, increased transcript levels are then perceived as stressful and trigger the retrograde response, culminating in a multifaceted stress phenotype.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that increased transcript levels correlate with retrograde response activation.

claim: COB protein levels are upregulated 9.3-fold in I0 as determined by quantitative label-free mass spectrometry.
source: We speculate in this regard that elevated protein levels of COB (I0: 9.3-fold; Mss116OE: 5.0-fold upregulation, as determined by quantitative label-free mass spectrometry) and COX1 (I0: 11.6-fold; Mss116OE: 12.1-fold upregulation) might interfere with proper assembly and function of complex III and complex IV, respectively, and therefore constitute a deleterious dosage imbalance phenotype.
evidence: Mass spectrometry measurement reported in the text.

claim: COB protein levels are upregulated 5.0-fold in Mss116OE as determined by quantitative label-free mass spectrometry.
source: We speculate in this regard that elevated protein levels of COB (I0: 9.3-fold; Mss116OE: 5.0-fold upregulation, as determined by quantitative label-free mass spectrometry) and COX1 (I0: 11.6-fold; Mss116OE: 12.1-fold upregulation) might interfere with proper assembly and function of complex III and complex IV, respectively, and therefore constitute a deleterious dosage imbalance phenotype.
evidence: Mass spectrometry measurement reported in the text.

evidence: Mass spectrometry measurement reported in the text.

evidence: Mass spectrometry measurement reported in the text.

claim: Elevated protein levels of COB and COX1 might interfere with proper assembly and function of complex III and complex IV, respectively, and therefore constitute a deleterious dosage imbalance phenotype.
source: We speculate in this regard that elevated protein levels of COB (I0: 9.3-fold; Mss116OE: 5.0-fold upregulation, as determined by quantitative label-free mass spectrometry) and COX1 (I0: 11.6-fold; Mss116OE: 12.1-fold upregulation) might interfere with proper assembly and function of complex III and complex IV, respectively, and therefore constitute a deleterious dosage imbalance phenotype.
evidence: Speculation about the mechanism by which elevated protein levels cause stress.

claim: Disruption of splicing homeostasis can impact normal physiological function and lead to cellular stress and disease.
source: It is now well documented that disruption of splicing homeostasis can impact normal physiological function and lead to cellular stress and disease (Wang and Cooper, 2007).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Splicing factor one is a modulator of dietary restriction-induced longevity in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: There is also increasingly detailed mechanistic knowledge of how proteins involved in splicing can alter growth and ageing via a metabolic route, exemplified by the recent finding that splicing factor one is a modulator of dietary restriction-induced longevity in Caenorhabditis elegans (Heintz et al., 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The classic model is that loss of splicing homeostasis leads to deleterious shifts in splice isoform production or precipitates increased production of erroneous transcripts.
source: The classic model here is that loss of splicing homeostasis – through genetic, developmental, or environmental perturbation – leads to deleterious shifts in splice isoform production or precipitates increased production of erroneous transcripts that tax the quality control system and/or have direct cytotoxic effects.
evidence: Summary of established models in the field.

claim: In the classic model, the disease/stress state is a high-error state.
source: In other words, the disease/stress state is a high-error state.
evidence: Summary of the classic model.

claim: Normal splicing can be associated with high error rates.
source: Our results are unusual in that they suggest that normal splicing can be associated with high error rates and that, therefore, splicing homeostasis can also be disturbed by increasing splicing efficacy.
evidence: Inference based on the experimental results showing that increased splicing efficiency causes stress.

claim: Splicing homeostasis can be disturbed by increasing splicing efficacy.
source: Our results are unusual in that they suggest that normal splicing can be associated with high error rates and that, therefore, splicing homeostasis can also be disturbed by increasing splicing efficacy.
evidence: Inference based on the experimental results showing that increased splicing efficiency causes stress.

claim: Some mitochondrial introns are fixed across extant S. cerevisiae populations whereas others exhibit presence/absence polymorphism.
source: It is evident from population genomic analysis of different S. cerevisiae strains that some mitochondrial introns are fixed across extant populations whereas others exhibit presence/absence polymorphism (Wolters et al., 2015).
evidence: Established knowledge from population genomic analysis supported by citation.

claim: The removal of at least some introns in isolation is insufficiently stressful to be purged by natural selection.
source: This seems to suggest that the removal of at least some introns in isolation is insufficiently stressful to be purged by natural selection.
evidence: Inference based on the observation of presence/absence polymorphism.

claim: Deletion of suv3 decreases levels of mature cox1/cob mRNA and compromises respiratory capacity.
source: At the same time, studies of suv3, the second DEAD box RNA helicase present in yeast mitochondria, suggest that the deleterious effect of deleting individual introns – while possibly idiosyncratic – is at least partially cumulative: deletion of suv3, a component of the mitochondrial degradosome, decreases levels of mature cox1/cob mRNA and compromises respiratory capacity, but less so where more introns had been removed from the mitochondrial DNA (Golik et al., 1995).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The effect of deleting suv3 on respiratory capacity is less severe where more introns had been removed from the mitochondrial DNA.
source: At the same time, studies of suv3, the second DEAD box RNA helicase present in yeast mitochondria, suggest that the deleterious effect of deleting individual introns – while possibly idiosyncratic – is at least partially cumulative: deletion of suv3, a component of the mitochondrial degradosome, decreases levels of mature cox1/cob mRNA and compromises respiratory capacity, but less so where more introns had been removed from the mitochondrial DNA (Golik et al., 1995).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: For the combinations tested, severity of suv3 deletion depends on the number but not identity of the cox1 or cob introns present.
source: Importantly – at least for the combinations tested – severity was found to depend on the number but not identity of the cox1 or cob introns present.
evidence: Established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Self-splicing introns are firmly embedded in the organization of mitochondrial gene expression such that removing them upsets proper expression of their host genes.
source: The phenotypic effects we observe run counter to the notion that self-splicing introns are low-cost passengers and instead demonstrate that at least some of these selfish elements are firmly embedded in the organization of mitochondrial gene expression such that removing them upsets proper expression of their host genes.
evidence: Inference based on the experimental results showing that intron removal causes stress.

claim: The observations can be explained by an evolutionary lock-in model where primordial colonization of an intron-free cox1/cob ancestor by a self-splicing intron led to a drop in cox1/cob mRNA levels and favoured compensatory mutations that increased cox1/cob transcription.
source: We suggest that our observations can be explained by an evolutionary lock-in model where the primordial colonization of an intron-free cox1/cob ancestor by a self-splicing intron led to a drop in cox1/cob mRNA levels and favoured compensatory mutations that increased cox1/cob transcription to restore mRNA abundances back to their original levels.
evidence: Proposed evolutionary model to explain the observations.

claim: When introns are forcibly removed, hard-wired upregulation of cox1/cob transcription turns maladaptive, leading to excess levels of mature mRNA.
source: When we forcibly remove these introns, however, this hard-wired upregulation turns maladaptive. There no longer is a pool of transcripts targeted for degradation leading to excess levels of mature mRNA.
evidence: Inference explaining the consequence of the evolutionary lock-in model.

claim: Self-splicing introns can spread despite substantial fitness costs.
source: However, since self-splicing introns can spread despite substantial fitness costs (Hickey, 1982), we do not actually need to evoke a cost-free ancestral event.
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Evolutionary lock-ins might provide an unappreciated mechanism to facilitate the longer term persistence of genetic parasites, especially in large host populations where evolution is not mutation-limited.
source: We suggest that evolutionary lock-ins of this type might provide an unappreciated mechanism to facilitate the longer term persistence of genetic parasites, especially in large host populations where evolution is not mutation-limited.
evidence: Speculation about the broader implications of the evolutionary lock-in model.

claim: For a given dosage-sensitive gene where failure to splice is common and transcription levels are set to compensate, intron loss might be deleterious and prevented by purifying selection even though the intron makes no adaptive contribution to gene regulation.
source: We also note that this argument might in principle extend to nuclear introns: if, for a given dosage-sensitive gene, failure to splice is common and transcription levels are set to compensate, intron loss might be deleterious and prevented by purifying selection even though the intron makes no adaptive contribution to gene regulation.
evidence: Speculation about the potential extension of the model to nuclear introns.

claim: Mobile genetic elements frequently compromise host fitness.
source: Mobile genetic elements frequently compromise host fitness (Werren, 2011), corrupting genetic information or disturbing adaptive gene expression patterns, sometimes to lethal effect.
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mobile genetic elements are ubiquitous in most eukaryotic genomes.
source: Despite this, mobile genetic elements are ubiquitous in most eukaryotic genomes (Hurst and Werren, 2001).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mobile elements can donate motifs (or domains) that are co-opted into host regulatory pathways (or genic sequence) over time.
source: Although mobile elements can donate motifs (or domains) that are co-opted into host regulatory pathways (or genic sequence) over time (Feschotte, 2008), deletions usually whittle away all but the core beneficial motif.
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Deletions usually whittle away all but the core beneficial motif of mobile elements.
source: Although mobile elements can donate motifs (or domains) that are co-opted into host regulatory pathways (or genic sequence) over time (Feschotte, 2008), deletions usually whittle away all but the core beneficial motif.
evidence: Established knowledge about the fate of mobile elements.

claim: Components that once mediated mobility of mobile elements, such as the reverse transcriptases of LINEs, are typically lost.
source: The components that once mediated mobility, such as the reverse transcriptases of long interspersed nuclear elements (LINEs), are typically lost.
evidence: Established knowledge about the fate of mobile elements.

claim: Functional selfish elements that remain mobile persist over evolutionary time because they replicate and spread to other sites in the genome faster than they are deleted.
source: Thus, functional selfish elements that remain mobile are thought to persist over evolutionary time not by virtue of sporadic beneficial effects for the host, but because they replicate and spread to other sites in the genome faster than they are deleted (Feschotte, 2008).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Self-splicing introns populate some highly expressed genes in archaea, bacteria, and organellar genomes of fungi and plants.
source: An interesting exception in this regard are self-splicing introns, which populate some highly expressed genes in archaea, bacteria, and organellar genomes of fungi and plants (Lambowitz and Belfort, 1993).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Self-splicing introns do not spawn a large pool of copies that disperse across the genome to escape mutational erasure.
source: In contrast to other mobile elements, self-splicing introns do not spawn a large pool of copies that disperse across the genome to escape mutational erasure.
evidence: Established knowledge about self-splicing introns.

claim: Owing to highly specific homing sites, each self-splicing intron is typically confined to a single location in the host genome.
source: Rather, owing to highly specific homing sites, each intron is typically confined to a single location in the host genome and evolutionary persistence seems to rely on continued re-invasion, either from other individuals in the same population (Goddard and Burt, 1999) or across species boundaries (Skelly and Maleszka, 1991; Dujon, 1989; Repar and Warnecke, 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge about self-splicing introns.

claim: Evolutionary persistence of self-splicing introns seems to rely on continued re-invasion, either from other individuals in the same population or across species boundaries.
source: Rather, owing to highly specific homing sites, each intron is typically confined to a single location in the host genome and evolutionary persistence seems to rely on continued re-invasion, either from other individuals in the same population (Goddard and Burt, 1999) or across species boundaries (Skelly and Maleszka, 1991; Dujon, 1989; Repar and Warnecke, 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Self-splicing introns can spread despite considerable fitness costs to the host.
source: Self-splicing introns can spread despite considerable fitness costs to the host (Hickey, 1982).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In practice, fitness costs of self-splicing introns might be relatively low as the host RNA is intact and fully functional once the intron has been spliced out.
source: However, in practice, fitness costs might be relatively low as the host RNA is intact and fully functional once the intron has been spliced out.
evidence: Established knowledge about self-splicing introns.

claim: Self-splicing introns do not contribute positively to host fitness.
source: As far as we know, self-splicing introns do not contribute positively to host fitness and, naively, one would expect that deleting these introns from the genome would be beneficial or, at worst, make no difference to the host.
evidence: Established knowledge about self-splicing introns.

claim: The S. cerevisiae mitochondrial genome contains 13 self-splicing introns.
source: Here, we investigate the consequences of deleting all 13 self-splicing introns from the S. cerevisiae mitochondrial genome
evidence: Stated in the introduction.

claim: The 21S ribosomal RNA gene Q0158 harbours a single group I intron named omega.
source: where they reside in three host genes: the 21S ribosomal RNA gene Q0158 (which harbours a single group I intron named omega)
evidence: Stated in the introduction.

claim: cox1 harbours group I introns aI3, aI4, aI5α, aI5β and group II introns aI1, aI2, aI5γ.
source: and two protein-coding genes, cox1 (group I: aI3, aI4, aI5α, aI5β; group II: aI1, aI2, aI5γ)
evidence: Stated in the introduction.

claim: cob harbours group I introns bI2, bI3, bI4, bI5 and group II intron bI1.
source: and cob (group I: bI2, bI3, bI4, bI5; group II: bI1)
evidence: Stated in the introduction.

claim: cox1 and cob both encode components of the electron transport chain.
source: and two protein-coding genes, cox1 (group I: aI3, aI4, aI5α, aI5β; group II: aI1, aI2, aI5γ) and cob (group I: bI2, bI3, bI4, bI5; group II: bI1), both encoding components of the electron transport chain.
evidence: Established knowledge about gene function.

claim: Timely splicing of self-splicing introns in vivo often depends on one or several trans-factors.
source: Note here, that we use 'self-splicing introns' as a convenient shorthand to describe the complete collection of group I and group II introns, even though timely splicing in vivo often depends on one or several trans-factors (see below) (Lambowitz and Belfort, 1993).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Removing mitochondrial introns has dramatic consequences for mitochondrial physiology and function.
source: We show that, contrary to expectations, removing these introns has dramatic consequences for mitochondrial physiology and function, triggering changes in nuclear gene expression that affect organismal growth and lifespan.
evidence: Summary of experimental results.

claim: Removing mitochondrial introns triggers changes in nuclear gene expression that affect organismal growth and lifespan.
source: We show that, contrary to expectations, removing these introns has dramatic consequences for mitochondrial physiology and function, triggering changes in nuclear gene expression that affect organismal growth and lifespan.
evidence: Summary of experimental results.

claim: The presence of mitochondrial self-splicing introns has become integral to normal mitochondrial gene expression.
source: Our results demonstrate that the presence of mitochondrial self-splicing introns has become integral to normal mitochondrial gene expression and that, curiously, normal mitochondrial function in S. cerevisiae has come to require inefficient splicing.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental results.

claim: Normal mitochondrial function in S. cerevisiae has come to require inefficient splicing.
source: Our results demonstrate that the presence of mitochondrial self-splicing introns has become integral to normal mitochondrial gene expression and that, curiously, normal mitochondrial function in S. cerevisiae has come to require inefficient splicing.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental results.

claim: Group II introns are known for low splicing efficiency, even in the presence of auxiliary proteins.
source: Group II introns in particular are known for low splicing efficiency, even in the presence of auxiliary proteins (Karunatilaka et al., 2010).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Strain a161 and a161-U7 are isogenic with regard to their nuclear genomes except for a single marker gene, ura3.
source: To test whether the removal of self-splicing mitochondrial introns affects host physiology and fitness, we compared two S. cerevisiae strains that are isogenic with regard to their nuclear genomes (except for a single marker gene, ura3, see Materials and methods) but differ with respect to mitochondrial intron content.
evidence: Description of experimental design.

claim: The omega intron is present in some yeast strains but absent in others without obvious phenotypic effects.
source: As previous work had found the omega intron to be 'optional' – present in some yeast strains but absent in others without obvious phenotypic effects (Wolters et al., 2015; Dujon, 1980)
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.
